title: Minor Scales
intro: The minor mode lowers the third scale degree, and usually the sixth and seventh too. Because the lowered seventh weakens the pull to the tonic, minor comes in three forms: natural, harmonic and melodic.

blocks.text: The natural minor scale follows W H W W H W W. A natural minor is the white keys from A to A. Compared with the major scale on the same tonic, it lowers 3̂, 6̂ and 7̂ by a semitone: C natural minor is C D E♭ F G A♭ B♭ C.

With a lowered 7̂ there is a whole step below the tonic and no leading tone, so the dominant chord is minor and the cadence is weak. Harmonic minor raises 7̂ back to a leading tone: A B C D E F G♯ A. The raised seventh makes a major dominant chord (E–G♯–B in A minor), but leaves an augmented second (three semitones) between 6̂ and 7̂, F–G♯, which gives the scale its 'exotic' sound.

To smooth that augmented second in melodies, melodic minor raises both 6̂ and 7̂ when the line rises (A B C D E F♯ G♯ A) and uses natural minor when it falls (A G F E D C B A). In jazz the ascending form is used both ways and called the 'jazz minor' scale.

widget.title: The three forms of A minor

items: Relative keys share a key signature: C major and A minor (no sharps or flats), G major and E minor (one sharp). The relative minor's tonic is 6̂ of the major scale, a minor third below the major tonic.
Parallel keys share a tonic: C major and C minor. Composers often borrow chords from the parallel key (see Chromatic Harmony).

blocks.text: A piece in a minor key does not pick one of the three forms and stick to it. It uses natural-minor 6̂ and 7̂ in falling lines and over subdominant harmony, and raised 6̂ and 7̂ in rising lines and in the dominant chord. The 'three scales' are a summary of how the two variable degrees behave.

items: Step 1. Play A natural minor with the right hand: A to A on the white keys only, fingering 1 2 3 1 2 3 4 5 (thumb under after C).
Step 2. Play it again with G♯ instead of G near the top: that is harmonic minor. Listen for the wide step F to G♯.
Step 3. Now play F♯ and G♯ going up, and F and G coming down: melodic minor.
Step 4. Play A major (with C♯, F♯, G♯) straight after A minor and compare: the C♮/C♯ (the third) is the biggest change.
Step 5. Find the relative major of A minor: it uses the same white keys from C. Play C major then A minor and hear the same notes with a different home.

blocks.title: Relative minor
blocks.text: What is the relative minor of E♭ major, and of A major?
solution: The relative minor starts on 6̂, a minor third below the tonic. E♭ major: 6̂ is C, so C minor (three flats). A major: 6̂ is F♯, so F♯ minor (three sharps).

blocks.title: Harmonic minor
blocks.text: Write D harmonic minor and name its augmented second.
solution: D natural minor: D E F G A B♭ C. Raise 7̂: C♯. D harmonic minor: D E F G A B♭ C♯ D. The augmented second is B♭–C♯.
blocks.answer: D E F G A B♭ C♯ D; B♭–C♯
